prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks, in which magic-wavelength trapping of many neutral atoms led to atomic timekeeping at the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: I keep the single-part prize for optical lattice clocks, and round 1 has strengthened rather than weakened my reason. The scientific claim is specific: Katori's magic-wavelength lattice cancels the light shift on the clock transition so that very many atoms can be interrogated at once, and the realizations, above all Ye's strontium clocks, reached fractional uncertainties near 10^-18 and opened many-body clock physics. Strontium and ytterbium clocks in several national laboratories reproduce the performance and have been compared across continents, so maturity is not the issue. The uses are measurable: bounds on drifting constants, relativistic geodesy and the preparation for a redefinition of the second. My deciding point is that the chair's summary shows all eight members describe the same two-name allocation, while the Higgs ballots have produced three different trios. I read that as evidence about the credit, not as a vote count. Exact credit is half of the Nobel test, and B013 is the only shortlisted entry where I can state it in one sentence without leaving out someone I would have to defend leaving out. I had also made a factual slip in round 1: I wrote that Pearce dropped Jenni, but the chair's summary shows Pearce credits Gianotti, Jenni and Virdee. The three Higgs trios still differ, but the disagreement is narrower than I said: Gianotti and Jenni are common, and the open seat is Virdee versus Della Negra.
statement.case_against: The strongest objection is still overlap and the weight of the Higgs result. The 2005 prize covered the frequency comb and the 2012 prize ion control, so a sceptic reads lattice clocks as a very good refinement of honoured metrology. The Higgs observation is the larger result for physics as a whole, and its experimental half has been unrecognised since 2013; Mehlig and Olsson both say passing over it has a real cost, and I accept that. The redefinition of the second has not yet happened, and Katori and Ye do not reflect the contributions of Lemonde and the Paris group, Lisdat, Sterr, Takamoto and the NIST and JILA teams, or the ion-clock pioneers. I would answer by wording the citation around the invention of the magic-wavelength lattice clock and its realization at 10^-18, not around optical clocks in general. That is the part not contained in the comb or ion-control work. I do not claim this removes the overlap objection; it narrows it.

responses.point: Pearce, as chair, rests the Higgs case on the science and not on the tally, calls the discovery mature for years, and treats Virdee and Della Negra as close to interchangeable on the supplied evidence, while acknowledging that crediting collaboration leaders is the weak point.
responses.response: I agree with every scientific statement in his case, and I do not dispute that the Higgs observation is the more consequential result. Our disagreement is only about credit. If Virdee and Della Negra are interchangeable on the evidence, that is the problem: a prize should not depend on a choice the committee itself calls arbitrary between two people with similar claims. Pearce's reply to the chair's question is the one that would change my mind: a stated principle (founders at conception versus spokespersons at announcement) applied the same way to ATLAS and CMS and that the supporters accept as one trio. Without that, I would rather give an unarguable prize than an arguable one. If such a principle emerges, I would still rank B001 above my other alternatives, which is why it is my first fallback.

responses.point: Johansson ranks the Higgs first with Gianotti, Della Negra and Jenni, admits that choosing three of four is a judgement call that omits Virdee, and says B013 is a fallback if no trio can be agreed.
responses.response: His trio differs from Pearce's and Danielsson's in exactly one seat, and he states openly that the choice is not a verified accounting. That is the honest position, but it is also the case against a final public position on B001 today. Three supporters of one prize with two trios among them is not a configuration the committee can state, and I do not think a recorded vote can supply the principle that the science does not. I note and welcome his offer of B013 as a fallback; it means the room is closer than the first-place labels suggest. As in round 1, I think his link to circuit QED should keep B054 out of his advocacy, and I do not read it as bearing on B013 or B001.

responses.point: Olsson prefers B013 for defensible attribution, not because it outweighs the Higgs observation, and lists the Higgs as a possible outranking if a three-name allocation can be defended.
responses.response: I share her framing exactly: B013 is chosen because its invention and its people can be named, not because it is bigger. I would also hold her reading of 'invention' as the test for the citation. If the committee writes the citation around the magic-wavelength lattice and the 10^-18 realization, the 2005 and 2012 overlap becomes a statement about lineage, not a repetition. Where I differ slightly is that she treats the Higgs as capable of outranking B013 once a trio is defensible; I would only accept that if the trio rests on one principle that also covers the CMS and ATLAS founders, not on a case-by-case choice.

responses.point: Kroll ranks B013 first and says it follows from the 2005 and 2012 prizes without repeating them, and the chair's summary records his disclosed possible tie to John Hall's laboratory, with which Jun Ye is associated, and his suggestion that the committee consider recusal on B013.
responses.response: I would keep the disclosure on the record and let the committee decide on recusal, but I would not make the case for B013 depend on his ballot. Five of us hold B013 as first choice and a recusal by Kroll would leave four, still the largest group, and the ranking reasons I gave do not rest on his argument. On substance, 'follows without repeating' is more than I can claim: lattice clocks use comb and ultrastable-laser techniques honoured in 2005, so the word 'repeating' invites the objection. My own ground is narrower and I think safer: magic-wavelength trapping is the distinct step.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will accept optical lattice clocks as a distinct invention rather than a continuation of the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes.
Whether a single principle for choosing three of the four Higgs leaders can be agreed, in which case B001 may outrank B013 on significance and I would reconsider.
Whether the redefinition of the second will be decided or firmly scheduled before the decision, and whether the committee should wait for it.
Relative credit of Katori's proposal and Ye's realization, and of other lattice-clock groups, which I recall from general knowledge and not from verified sources.
statement.conflict_note: No personal or institutional conflict with the credited names Katori and Ye is apparent from my profile. My documented connections (Uppsala Materials Theory, my doctoral supervisor Borje Johansson, Los Alamos, co-authors of my books) do not involve them. I have subject-matter closeness to the electronic-structure side of B043, B044 and B046, which I have disclosed and which I discount; none of these is in my preferred configuration. I also agree with the chair's record that Kroll's tie is a perceived one that the committee should note, and that my position on B013 does not depend on his ballot.
